title: Reverse an array (swap first with last, second with second-last, using two pointers).
keyPoints: Use two pointers, one at each end, swap the elements they point to, and move both inward until they meet.
The algorithm is O(n) time and O(1) extra space because it swaps in place with a single temporary variable.
The loop runs n/2 times because each swap fixes two elements.
An odd-length array handles itself naturally because the middle element stays in place when the pointers meet.
In-place reversal mutates the original array, which is a deliberate API decision that must be documented.
This two-pointer swap is the foundation for rotation, palindrome checks, and many array manipulation problems.

s1_definition.oneliner: Swap the two ends and move inward with two pointers until they meet, reversing the array in place.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Two-pointer technique** – one pointer starts at the left end, one at the right end.
- **Swap and step** – swap the two elements, then move left pointer right and right pointer left.
- **Stop condition** – continue while `left < right`; when they meet, every element is in its mirrored position.
- **O(n) time** – the loop runs n/2 times, each doing a constant-time swap.
- **O(1) space** – only one temporary variable is needed for the swap, no second array is allocated.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh has a printed statement where transactions are listed oldest first, but he wants newest first. He puts one finger on the top line and one on the bottom line, swaps those two lines, then moves both fingers inward by one and swaps again. He keeps going until his fingers meet in the middle. Now the whole statement is reversed without needing a second sheet of paper.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing an array is a textbook two-pointer problem that I solve in place. I put one pointer at the left end and one at the right end, swap the two elements they point at, then move the left pointer one step right and the right pointer one step left. I keep going while the left pointer is still before the right pointer. When they meet in the middle, the whole array is reversed.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this when displaying statements. The database stores Rajesh's transactions oldest first, but the mobile app needs to show the newest transactions at the top. Rather than issuing a second expensive sorted query or building a whole new array, I reverse the list in place inside the service layer.

The in-place aspect is what I emphasise in an interview, because the naive solution creates a brand new array and copies elements backwards, which doubles the memory. On a phone displaying a long statement that extra memory matters, so the two-pointer swap that needs only one temporary variable is the professional choice.

Remember one sentence: two pointers at both ends, swap and step inward, stop when they meet.
